y-m-49-01.title: Two of the same conditions: does the relationship change when the base changes?
y-m-49-01.topic: Necessary and sufficient conditions (a judgment that depends on the universal set)
y-m-49-01.goal: Judge the necessary and sufficient relation of two conditions by examining the two 'if ... then' directions, and explain how new information (the full shape of the solutions, a change of universal set) changes the judgment.
y-m-49-01.material:
There are two conditions about a real number x.
p: x²−3x+2=0 (x squared minus 3x plus 2 equals 0)
q: x=1
If 'if p then q' is true, p is a sufficient condition for q, and if 'if q then p' is true, p is a necessary condition for q. If both are true, it is a necessary and sufficient condition. The universal set at first is all real numbers.
y-m-49-01.thinking.0: Hold off on a judgment when evidence is lacking
y-m-49-01.thinking.1: Know that one direction is false from a counterexample
y-m-49-01.thinking.2: Know that the truth of a condition depends on the universal set
y-m-49-01.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-01.prereq.1: Solving the quadratic equation x²−3x+2=0 by factoring (middle school level)
y-m-49-01.prereq.2: That for 'if p then q' to be true, every x that satisfies p must satisfy q
y-m-49-01.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step choose a judgment, and when new information comes out, check that judgment again.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write all the x that satisfy p and q.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.hint.1: Check separately whether there is an x that breaks 'if p then q' and whether there is an x that breaks 'if q then p'.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Minseo put x=1 into the two conditions, and both p and q were true.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: From the information so far, what kind of condition would you judge p to be for q?
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Just knowing that the single value x=1 satisfies both conditions confirms none of the 'if ... then' directions. One example holding does not show truth for all x.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: p is a sufficient condition for q but not a necessary condition
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: It has not yet been confirmed whether 'if p then q' is true for all x. Both being true at one value does not tell the direction.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: p is a necessary condition for q but not a sufficient condition
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: There is not yet any basis that only 'if q then p' is true. A single x=1 cannot check 'all x'.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: p is a necessary and sufficient condition for q
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: We still do not know whether the two conditions are satisfied by exactly the same values (whether they are the same set). One value matching is no evidence of that.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: With the current information it is hard to decide which one it is
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment that points out that both being true at one value decides neither of the two directions.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Rewriting the expression of p as (x−1)(x−2)=0, the real numbers x satisfying p are 1 and 2. The only real number x satisfying q is 1. (The universal set is still all real numbers.)
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at the new information, judge again what kind of condition p is for q.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.after: x=2 makes only p true, so 'if p then q' is false (not a sufficient condition), and x=1, which satisfies q, also satisfies p, so 'if q then p' is true (a necessary condition).
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: p is a sufficient condition for q but not a necessary condition
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Examine 'if p then q' for x=2. p is true, but what about q?
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: p is a necessary condition for q but not a sufficient condition
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a judgment made by looking together at two facts: x=2 satisfies only p, and x=1, which satisfies q, satisfies p as well.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: p is a necessary and sufficient condition for q
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Compare whether the x that satisfy p are exactly the same as the x that satisfy q. Is there no value other than 1?
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: With the current information it is hard to decide which one it is
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Now the solutions of both conditions are out. It is information that lets you examine each direction directly.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.info: The problem was fixed and the universal set became 'all real numbers that are 1 or less'. (The expressions of p and q stay the same.)
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now that the universal set has changed, judge what kind of condition p is for q.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Among real numbers that are 1 or less, 1 is the only x satisfying p, so the truth sets of p and q become equal. Even with the same two conditions, the necessary and sufficient relation can change when the universal set changes.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: p is a sufficient condition for q but not a necessary condition
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check whether x=2 is still in the universal set.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: p is a necessary condition for q but not a sufficient condition
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a judgment that used x=2 as a counterexample. Check whether x=2 can still be used in the changed universal set.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: p is a necessary and sufficient condition for q
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment made by checking whether the x satisfying p and q form the same set within the universal set.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: With the current information it is hard to decide which one it is
y-m-49-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: It is information that lets you decide, because you can find the solutions of p and q directly in the changed universal set too.
y-m-49-01.s.s1.reflect: Saying 'hard to decide' at first was reasonable because the information was lacking, and in the second step the counterexample x=2 decided the direction. In the third step, even with the same expressions, the universal set changed and so the judgment changed. Point out whether the reason your judgment changed was 'new information'.
y-m-49-01.s.s2.prompt: In one or two sentences, write why the judgment changed in step 3, connecting it to what happened to the value that was the counterexample in step 2.
y-m-49-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write what value of x broke 'if p then q' in step 2.
y-m-49-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether that value is inside the universal set of step 3.
y-m-49-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your writing show 'why x=2 is no longer a counterexample'?
y-m-49-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish that what changed is not the expressions but the universal set?
y-m-49-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you state the result (necessary and sufficient) together with the reason?
y-m-49-01.s.s2.model.0: x=2 was a counterexample because it satisfies p but not q, but when the universal set becomes the real numbers 1 or less, x=2 is not in the universal set, so the counterexample disappears. So both directions are true and it becomes a necessary and sufficient condition.
y-m-49-01.s.s2.model.1: Even though the expressions stay the same, x=2 does not belong to the new universal set, so 1 is the only value that satisfies p. Since p and q are satisfied by the same value only, the relationship changed.
y-m-49-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: A way of explaining as 'only 1' without writing the counterexample's value directly. The number 2 is included.

y-m-49-02.title: Can we say 'true' after checking a few examples?
y-m-49-02.topic: A proposition and its contrapositive (the basis for judging true or false)
y-m-49-02.goal: Find out that 'checking a few examples' cannot be a basis for judging true with the contrapositive, and make for yourself an integer x that shows the proposition is false.
y-m-49-02.material:
A proposition R about a real number x: 'If x²>4, then x>2.' (If x squared is greater than 4, then x is greater than 2.)
Mina wrote the following using the contrapositive to find out whether R is true. An original proposition and its contrapositive always have the same truth value.
y-m-49-02.thinking.0: Find the line with a lack of basis in the working
y-m-49-02.thinking.1: Make a counterexample yourself to show the proposition is false
y-m-49-02.thinking.2: Use the property that an original proposition and its contrapositive have the same truth value
y-m-49-02.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-02.prereq.1: That the contrapositive of 'if p then q' is 'if not q then not p', and it has the same truth value as the original proposition
y-m-49-02.prereq.2: That the solution of x²>4 is x<−2 or x>2 (basics of quadratic inequalities)
y-m-49-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Mina's working with the weakest basis.
y-m-49-02.s.s1.hint.0: Give each line a name for 'what the line does' (definition, transformation, checking, conclusion).
y-m-49-02.s.s1.line.0: The hypothesis of R is x²>4, and the conclusion is x>2.
y-m-49-02.s.s1.line.1: The contrapositive of R is 'If x≤2, then x²≤4.'
y-m-49-02.s.s1.line.2: Putting in x=2, x=1, x=0 gives x² of 4, 1, 0, all of which are 4 or less, so the contrapositive is true.
y-m-49-02.s.s1.line.3: The contrapositive is true, so R is also true.
y-m-49-02.s.s1.explain: It is line 3. The three values x=2, 1, 0 holding is not a basis for it holding for 'all real numbers x≤2'. For example, x=−3 is x≤2 but x²=9>4, so the contrapositive is false, and therefore R is also false. Line 2 (using the contrapositive) and line 4 (the contrapositive and the original proposition being the same) are correct.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.prompt: We want to show that R is false. Make two different integers x for which the hypothesis 'x²>4' is true and the conclusion 'x>2' is false.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write the range of x for which the hypothesis is true. Is it only on the positive side?
y-m-49-02.s.s2.hint.1: Look for values in that range where the conclusion 'x>2' is false.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The hypothesis x²>4 is not true. (x² must be greater than 4)
y-m-49-02.s.s2.fail.c3: If x>2, the conclusion is true too, so it cannot be a counterexample.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.explain: x=−3 has x²=9>4 and also x≤2. For the same reason −4, −5, … are all counterexamples too. If there is even one counterexample, R is false, and the contrapositive, which has the same truth value as the original proposition, is also false.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why Mina's line 3 is not enough as a basis for the contrapositive being true, using the value of x you made above.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the value of x you made above directly in the sentence.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare the three values Mina checked with the value you made. What is different?
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your writing include a specific value of x (a counterexample)?
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you make it clear that 'holding for a few ≠ holding for all x'?
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.model.0: She only checked the three values x=2, 1, 0 and did not check all values with x≤2. There are values like x=−3 where x≤2 but x²=9>4, so the contrapositive is false too.
y-m-49-02.s.s2.because.model.1: A few examples holding is not evidence that it holds for all x. Negative x was not checked, and −3 is a counterexample.
y-m-49-02.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, mark which range of numbers the values that line checked covered completely.

y-m-49-03.title: Club headcount survey: what more do we need to know for the answer to be fixed?
y-m-49-03.topic: Number of elements of a set (sufficiency of information and the possible range)
y-m-49-03.goal: Recognize that the given headcount information alone does not fix the answer, sort out what extra information would fix it, and build the range of possible values yourself.
y-m-49-03.material:
All 30 students in one grade were surveyed on whether they joined the math club or the science club. 17 joined the math club A and 14 joined the science club B. A student may join both clubs, and there may be students who joined neither. The number of students who joined both and the number who joined neither are not known yet.
What we want to find: the number of students who joined neither club.
y-m-49-03.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is sufficient
y-m-49-03.thinking.1: Sort out whether extra information fixes the value to one
y-m-49-03.thinking.2: Build the range of possible cases yourself
y-m-49-03.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-03.prereq.1: The relation between the numbers of elements of two sets (the numbers of elements of the union and intersection)
y-m-49-03.prereq.2: The notation n(A) for the number of elements of a finite set
y-m-49-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the facts below such that knowing just 'one' of them fixes the number of students who joined neither club to a single value.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.hint.0: Call the number of overlapping students x, and write whether each fact becomes an equation in x.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.hint.1: Even if it becomes an equation, tell apart whether x is fixed to one value or only a range is fixed.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.o.a: At least 20 students joined at least one of the two clubs.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.r.a: Information that only gives a range, like '20 or more', does not fix the value to one. Check whether several possible values remain.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.o.b: 11 students in the math club did not join the science club.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a choice for examining whether this information can fix the number of overlapping students among the 17 in the math club.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.o.c: Adding the memberships of the two clubs gives 31.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.r.c: 17+14=31 is information given from the start. It does not tell whether overlapping students were counted twice.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.o.d: 19 students joined exactly one club only.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.r.d: You can judge by writing as an equation how the number of students who joined only one club is related to the number of overlapping students.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.o.e: Every science club student also joined the math club.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.r.e: An inclusion relation can fix the number of overlapping students directly. Think about the size of the intersection when one set is a subset of the other.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.o.f: There are students who joined both clubs.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.r.f: We can already know this fact from the point that 17+14=31 is greater than 30. It is not new information, and how many students overlap is still open.
y-m-49-03.s.s1.explain: If the number of overlapping students is x, the number who joined neither is 30−(31−x)=x−1. b gives 17−x=11 so x=6, d gives 31−2x=19 so x=6, and e says all 14 in the science club overlap, so x=14 is fixed. For a, c, and f, x is not fixed to one value.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.prompt: The first information alone does not fix the number of students who joined neither. Make two different possible cases. (x: the number of students who joined both clubs, y: the number who joined neither)
y-m-49-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one x and write whether math only, science only, both, and neither all come out as numbers of people.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check which box becomes strange if you set x to 0.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.var.x: Number of students who joined both clubs
y-m-49-03.s.s2.var.y: Number of students who joined neither club
y-m-49-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of students must be an integer.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of overlapping students is from 0 to 14 (the science club has 14).
y-m-49-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of overlapping students is 0 or more and cannot exceed the 14 in the science club.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The number of students who joined neither is 0 or more.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of students cannot be negative. Check that it does not exceed the total of 30.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.fail.c4: Math 17, science 14, overlap x, and the total of 30 do not fit together.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.explain: y=x−1 and x is from 1 to 14. If x=0, then y=−1, which is impossible; if x=1, then y=0; if x=14, then y=13. So from the first information alone, y can take several values from 0 to 13.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Based on the cases you made, write why the 'number of students who joined neither club' cannot be fixed from the first information alone, and the range that value can take.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare what y is when x is smallest and when x is largest.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: First write in one sentence how not knowing x connects to not knowing y.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you use as evidence that the two cases you made give different answers?
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Can you explain why the two ends of the range are those values (0 and 13)?
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.model.0: The number who joined both is not fixed, so the number who joined neither is not fixed either. If 1 student overlaps it is 0, and if 14 overlap it is 13, so it can be any value from 0 to 13.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.model.1: The size of the intersection can be anything from 1 to 14, so the answer is not fixed to one. The students who joined neither club are from 0 to 13.
y-m-49-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: A way that wrote only the range and did not write the two examples separately.

y-m-49-04.title: If the common part with A is the same, are the two sets the same too?
y-m-49-04.topic: Operations on sets (if the intersections are equal, are the sets equal?)
y-m-49-04.goal: Build a counterexample showing 'If A∩B=A∩C, then B=C' is false, and sort out the extra conditions that guarantee B=C.
y-m-49-04.material:
The universal set is U={1, 2, 3, 4} and A={1, 2}. A claim T about subsets B and C of U:
'If A∩B=A∩C, then B=C.'
When you make B and C below, write 1 in the boxes b1 to b4 if each element 1, 2, 3, 4 belongs to B and 0 if it does not, and write C the same way in the boxes c1 to c4. (e.g., if B={1, 3}, then b1=1, b2=0, b3=1, b4=0)
y-m-49-04.thinking.1: Find out that elements outside A do not show up in the intersection
y-m-49-04.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-04.prereq.1: Definitions of the intersection, union, and difference of sets
y-m-49-04.prereq.2: Subsets and the meaning of two sets being equal (each includes the other)
y-m-49-04.s.s1.prompt: Make two different pairs B, C that show T does not hold. (A∩B=A∩C but B≠C. A pair with B and C swapped counts as the same example.)
y-m-49-04.s.s1.hint.0: First decide whether elements 1 and 2 belong to B and C, and make A∩B and A∩C equal.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.hint.1: Then find which element (1 to 4) has a box where you can make B and C different.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.fail.c1: In each box write only 0 (does not belong) or 1 (belongs).
y-m-49-04.s.s1.ok.c2: The common part with A (elements 1, 2) is the same.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.fail.c2: A∩B and A∩C are not equal. Whether elements 1 and 2 belong must be the same in B and C.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.ok.c3: B and C are different from each other.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.fail.c3: B and C are the same set. There must be at least one element that differs.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.explain: For example, if B={1, 3} and C={1, 4}, then A∩B=A∩C={1} but B≠C. Also B={2}, C={2, 3, 4} gives A∩B=A∩C={2} but B≠C. There is a counterexample, so T is false.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.prompt: In the two examples you made, are the elements where B and C differ inside A or outside A? Use this to write why T does not hold.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.hint.0: In each of the two examples, write what element B and C differ in.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.hint.1: After checking whether that element belongs to A, if it does, think about what A∩B and A∩C become.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you point out exactly the elements that differ in your two examples?
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words the reason 'an intersection only looks at elements inside A'?
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.model.0: B and C differ only in elements 3 and 4. 3 and 4 do not belong to A, so they do not show up in the common part with A. So even if A∩B=A∩C, B≠C can happen, and T is false.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.model.1: The common part is compared only inside A, so we cannot tell even if elements outside A differ. For example, if B={1,3} and C={1,4}, only 3 and 4 outside A differ, so it is a counterexample.
y-m-49-04.s.s1.because.modelNote.1: A way that gave specific sets.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.prompt: When A∩B=A∩C holds, choose all the conditions that, added to it, 'always' guarantee B=C.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.hint.0: For each condition, find one example with B≠C. If you can find one, that condition does not guarantee it.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.hint.1: Split into 'inside A' and 'outside A' and examine whether B and C are the same.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.o.a: A⊂B (A is a subset of B)
y-m-49-04.s.s2.r.a: Even if A is inside B, elements outside A are still free in B and C. Check B={1, 2, 3}, C={1, 2, 4}.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.r.b: The condition of being disjoint is actually far from B and C being equal. Check whether B={3}, C={4} fits this condition.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.r.c: Think about whether the unions being equal is information that tells what B and C are like outside A.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.o.d: n(B)=n(C) (the numbers of elements are the same)
y-m-49-04.s.s2.r.d: Having the same number of elements does not mean having the same elements. Check B={3}, C={4}.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.o.e: B−A=C−A (the parts not belonging to A are the same)
y-m-49-04.s.s2.r.e: Think about whether, if the elements outside A are the same and the elements inside A are the same, B and C are entirely the same.
y-m-49-04.s.s2.explain: c: If x∈B, then whether or not x belongs to A, x∈A∪B=A∪C, and if it belongs to A, x∈C because A∩B=A∩C, and if it is outside A, x∈C (the reverse is the same). e means B and C are the same, with inside A by A∩B=A∩C and outside A by B−A=C−A. a, b, and d have counterexamples such as B={3}, C={4} or B={1,2,3}, C={1,2,4}.

y-m-49-05.title: n²+n+41: how many values must we check before we can believe it?
y-m-49-05.topic: Truth and negation of propositions (counterexamples of propositions with 'all')
y-m-49-05.goal: Know that the number of examples that hold does not make a proof for a proposition with 'all', judge that one counterexample makes it false, and write the negation of that proposition correctly.
y-m-49-05.material:
Proposition R: 'For every natural number n, n²+n+41 is a prime number.' (n squared plus n plus forty-one)
A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself.
y-m-49-05.thinking.0: Judge the limits of inductive evidence
y-m-49-05.thinking.1: Hold off or update a judgment as evidence grows
y-m-49-05.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-05.prereq.1: Meaning of a prime number (a natural number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself)
y-m-49-05.prereq.2: The expressions 'for all ...' and 'for some ...' and negation (basics of high school Common Math)
y-m-49-05.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose your judgment about R.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the number of n checked so far with the range of n that R talks about.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write what kind of n, even just one, is needed for R to be false.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.info: When n=1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the values of n²+n+41 are 43, 47, 53, 61, 71, and all are prime.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: How would you judge R (for every natural number n, n²+n+41 is prime) now?
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Five being prime does not mean it is prime for all n. With no counterexample, 'it may be true, we do not know yet' is reasonable.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: True. It has not been wrong even once where we checked
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Holding five times is not checking 'every natural number n'. There are unchecked n left.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It may be true, but we cannot settle it yet
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a choice that held off the judgment by separating the range checked from the range not checked.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: False. It is suspicious from the checking so far
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: No counterexample has appeared, so declaring it false also needs a basis. Did you find even one counterexample?
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.info: A computer checked all 39 values from n=1 to 39, and all were prime.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at this information, decide your judgment about R again.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.after: Even when more examples hold, 'for all n' is not settled without a proof. Your degree of confidence has gone up, but the judgment can stay as 'not settled'.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: True. It has not been wrong even once where we checked
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Checking 39 is not checking the 40th and beyond. Even if the number checked is large, it cannot show 'all'.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It may be true, but we cannot settle it yet
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is the judgment that confidence has gone up, but as long as there are unchecked n, it is not settled.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: False. It is suspicious from the checking so far
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Not one counterexample has appeared yet. What would be needed to call it false?
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Looking at this information, decide your judgment about R.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.after: n=40 is a counterexample. A proposition of the form 'all ... are ...' becomes false with one counterexample, and the fact that the earlier 39 held does not make R true.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check directly whether the value at n=40 is prime. Examine the divisors of 1681.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It may be true, but we cannot settle it yet
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If 1681 is not prime, think about whether R has any reason left to stay on hold.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that used the fact that a claim about 'all n' breaks as soon as even one non-prime value appears.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.reflect: In the first two steps it was fine to leave 'not settled yet' as it was (only the degree of confidence changed). The counterexample in the third step changed the kind of judgment. Was it 'because there were more examples' or 'because a counterexample appeared' that you changed your judgment?
y-m-49-05.s.s2.prompt: Which is the right negation of R?
y-m-49-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put into words the situation where R is false: how many n must be non-prime?
y-m-49-05.s.s2.hint.1: Check directly what value each choice gives for 1 to 39.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.o.a: For some natural number n, n²+n+41 is a prime number.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.r.a: This lists the cases where R is true. A negation is a statement that holds when R is false.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.o.b: For some natural number n, n²+n+41 is not a prime number.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.r.b: This is a choice that pointed out that this form is needed for 'all ... are ...' to be false.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.o.c: For every natural number n, n²+n+41 is not a prime number.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.r.c: This is the case that changed the negation of 'all ... are ...' into 'all ... are not ...'. For n with 1≤n≤39 it is prime. Examine whether this statement is the same as R being false.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.o.d: Only when n=40, n²+n+41 is not a prime number.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.r.d: This is the case that treated one specific counterexample as the negation. A negation is a general statement that covers any n that is a counterexample.
y-m-49-05.s.s2.explain: The negation of 'for all n, P(n)' is 'for some n, P(n) is not true'. n=40 is an example (a counterexample) that makes this negation true.
y-m-49-05.s.s3.prompt: Write why n=40 alone makes R false, and why all of 1 to 39 being prime is not evidence that R is true.
y-m-49-05.s.s3.hint.0: Put n=40 into the expression to find the value, and find the divisors of that value.
y-m-49-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the range covered by 39 holding with the range of 'all natural numbers' holding.
y-m-49-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Do both 'one is enough' and 'many is not enough' show in your writing?
y-m-49-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check why n=40 is not prime (1681=41×41)?
y-m-49-05.s.s3.model.0: n=40 is a counterexample, so R is false. A proposition about 'all n' breaks with one counterexample, and even if 39 hold, it can break at the 40th.
y-m-49-05.s.s3.model.1: 1681=41×41, so it is not prime, and so with just one n=40, 'all n' does not hold. No matter how many examples that hold you collect, it is not a proof that it holds for all n.
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: True. It was never wrong from 1 to 39
y-m-49-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: False. One value that is not a prime came out

y-m-49-06.title: Proofs written by four students: which writing showed S?
y-m-49-06.topic: Proof of a proposition (proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, and telling it apart from the converse)
y-m-49-06.goal: Sort out which of four writings is accepted as a proof, and explain what a writing with the hypothesis and conclusion swapped proves.
y-m-49-06.material:
A proposition S about natural numbers a and b: 'If ab is odd, then a and b are both odd.'
Four students each wrote that they proved S.
가: If a=3, b=5, then ab=15 is odd, and a and b are both odd. If a=7, b=9, then ab=63 is odd, and both are odd. Therefore S is true.
나: Suppose at least one of a and b is even. If we call that even number 2k (k is a natural number), then ab has 2k as a factor, so it is even. Therefore if ab is odd, then a and b are both odd.
다: Suppose a and b are both odd. If a=2m+1 and b=2n+1 (m and n are integers that are 0 or more), then ab=4mn+2m+2n+1=2(2mn+m+n)+1, so it is odd. Therefore S has been proved.
라: Suppose ab is odd and a is even. If a=2k, then ab=2kb is even. This contradicts the assumption that ab is odd, so a is odd. b is odd in the same way.
y-m-49-06.thinking.0: Compare and evaluate several ways of proving
y-m-49-06.thinking.2: Distinguish the converse from the original proposition
y-m-49-06.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-06.prereq.1: Writing an even number in the form 2k and an odd number in the form 2k+1 (k is an integer)
y-m-49-06.prereq.2: The meaning of proving by contrapositive and by contradiction
y-m-49-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the writings that can be accepted as having proved S.
y-m-49-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write where each writing starts from (what it assumes).
y-m-49-06.s.s1.hint.1: S is a proposition that assumes 'ab is odd'. Split the writings into those with the same assumption and those with a different one.
y-m-49-06.s.s1.r.a: Holding in a few examples cannot show a proposition about 'all natural numbers a, b'. Look at whether there is general logic that is not examples.
y-m-49-06.s.s1.r.b: This is a choice that pointed out why a writing that proves the contrapositive becomes a proof of the original proposition.
y-m-49-06.s.s1.r.c: Compare whether what this writing took as the hypothesis and what it showed as the conclusion are in the same order as the hypothesis and conclusion of S.
y-m-49-06.s.s1.r.d: This is a choice that pointed out the structure of proof by contradiction: if a result contradicting the assumption comes out, it shows the first assumption was wrong.
y-m-49-06.s.s1.explain: 나 proved the contrapositive of S ('if at least one is even, then ab is even'), and 라 proved it by contradiction. 가 is only checking examples, and 다 proved the 'converse', in which the hypothesis and conclusion are swapped.
y-m-49-06.s.s2.prompt: Explain why the writing 다 does not prove S using the words 'hypothesis' and 'conclusion', and also write what proposition this writing proved.
y-m-49-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the hypothesis and conclusion of S in one line each, and write the first line and last line of 다 in the same way.
y-m-49-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the hypothesis and conclusion of the two sides.
y-m-49-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the proposition that 다 proved exactly as 'If a and b are both odd, then ab is odd'?
y-m-49-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you also write what the hypothesis and conclusion of S are?
y-m-49-06.s.s2.model.0: 다 showed 'If a and b are both odd, then ab is odd'. This is the converse, with the hypothesis and conclusion of S swapped, so it does not show that S is right.
y-m-49-06.s.s2.model.1: S has to assume that ab is odd and show that a and b are odd, but 다 started the other way round, from a and b being odd. The direction is opposite, so it did not prove S.

y-m-49-07.title: Which condition of being a multiple of some number k fits?
y-m-49-07.topic: Necessary and sufficient conditions (divisor and multiple conditions)
y-m-49-07.goal: Make several k for which 'if it is a multiple of 60 then it is a multiple of k' is true but its converse is false, and explain with specific numbers why some k do not work.
y-m-49-07.material:
A condition about a natural number x, p: 'x is a multiple of 60.'
For a natural number k, consider the condition q_k: 'x is a multiple of k.' (e.g., if k=4, q_k is 'x is a multiple of 4') In this task, x ranges over all natural numbers.
y-m-49-07.thinking.0: Build a case where only one direction between conditions holds
y-m-49-07.thinking.1: Show that one direction is false with a counterexample
y-m-49-07.thinking.2: Grasp the range of solutions in a situation where several solutions are possible
y-m-49-07.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-07.prereq.2: That for 'if p then q' to be true, every number that satisfies p must satisfy q
y-m-49-07.s.s1.prompt: When k=4, which is the right relationship between p and q_k?
y-m-49-07.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether multiples of 60 such as x=60, 120, 180 are multiples of 4.
y-m-49-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write the multiples of 4 from the smallest and check whether any is not a multiple of 60.
y-m-49-07.s.s1.o.a: p is a necessary condition for q_k but not a sufficient condition
y-m-49-07.s.s1.r.a: You may have the direction backwards. First check whether 'if p then q_k' is true.
y-m-49-07.s.s1.o.b: p is a necessary and sufficient condition for q_k
y-m-49-07.s.s1.r.b: Check whether any multiple of 4 is not a multiple of 60. For example, how about x=4?
y-m-49-07.s.s1.o.c: p is a sufficient condition for q_k but not a necessary condition
y-m-49-07.s.s1.r.c: This is a choice that looked together at two facts: 'if p then q_k' is true, and 'if q_k then p' is false (e.g., x=4).
y-m-49-07.s.s1.o.d: p is neither a sufficient nor a necessary condition for q_k
y-m-49-07.s.s1.r.d: Check whether a multiple of 60 is a multiple of 4. Use 60=4×15.
y-m-49-07.s.s1.explain: A multiple of 60 is always a multiple of 4, so 'if p then q_k' is true. On the other hand, x=4 is a multiple of 4 but not a multiple of 60, so 'if q_k then p' is false. Therefore p is a sufficient condition for q_k and not a necessary condition.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.prompt: Make three different k for which 'if p then q_k' is true but 'if q_k then p' is false. (k is a natural number)
y-m-49-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write down a few multiples of 60 and find what relationship k must have with 60 for all of them to be multiples of k.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with k=60 and check whether any multiple of k is not a multiple of 60.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Every multiple of 60 is a multiple of k (k is a divisor of 60).
y-m-49-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Some multiple of 60 is not a multiple of k. 'If p then q_k' breaks.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.ok.c3: Some multiple of k is not a multiple of 60.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Every multiple of k becomes a multiple of 60. 'If q_k then p' becomes true.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.explain: For 'if a multiple of 60 then a multiple of k' to be true, k must be a divisor of 60, and for 'if a multiple of k then a multiple of 60' to be false, k must not be 60. So k is one of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30 (k=1 is also possible).
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why k=8 does not satisfy the condition above, by giving a multiple of 60 that is not a multiple of 8.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the multiples of 60 in the order 60, 120, 180, … and divide them by 8.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find one that is not divisible and put it into your sentence.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the number you gave really a multiple of 60?
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you show with that number that 'if p then q_k' is false?
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.model.0: x=60 is a multiple of 60 but not a multiple of 8. The statement that a multiple of 60 is a multiple of 8 is false, so k=8 is not allowed.
y-m-49-07.s.s2.because.model.1: Among the multiples of 60, 180 is not divisible by 8, so it is not a multiple of 8, and 'if p then q_k' does not hold.

y-m-49-08.title: Which line of the survey working went wrong?
y-m-49-08.topic: Number of elements of a set (checking the headcount calculation for a union, and contradictions in the data)
y-m-49-08.goal: Find the missing part in a headcount calculation, check that the given data does not contradict the total, and build survey results that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-49-08.material:
40 students in one class were asked which of English and math they like (there may be students who like both subjects, and students who like neither). The number of students who like English, A, is 25, the number who like math, B, is 18, and the number who like both subjects is 7.
Siu found 'the number of students who like neither subject' as shown below.
y-m-49-08.thinking.0: Find the error by checking the working line by line
y-m-49-08.thinking.1: Judge whether the data contradicts itself
y-m-49-08.thinking.2: Build data that satisfies the conditions
y-m-49-08.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-08.prereq.1: The relation between the numbers of elements of the union and intersection of two sets
y-m-49-08.prereq.2: Writing 'the number of elements that belong only to A' as n(A)−n(A∩B)
y-m-49-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first wrong line in Siu's working.
y-m-49-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write the headcount in the four regions (English only, math only, both, neither) and check whether the sum is 40.
y-m-49-08.s.s1.hint.1: Match the number found in each line with the region it belongs to. Is any region missing?
y-m-49-08.s.s1.line.2: Students who like at least one subject: 18+11=29 (students)
y-m-49-08.s.s1.explain: It is line 3. The students who like at least one subject include English only (18), math only (11), and both subjects (7), so 18+11+7=36 students. Siu left out the 7 students who like both subjects. Then 40−36=4 in line 4 is the correct answer. Lines 1 and 2 are correct.
y-m-49-08.s.s2.prompt: The survey results of another class are like this: 30 students in total, 20 like English, 15 like math, and 3 like both subjects. Which is the right judgment about this data?
y-m-49-08.s.s2.hint.0: Find what 20+15−3 is and compare it with the total of 30.
y-m-49-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find the headcounts of English only, math only, and both, and check their sum.
y-m-49-08.s.s2.o.a: It is possible. If there are students who like both subjects, the headcount is less than 20+15
y-m-49-08.s.s2.r.a: It is right to account for the overlap. Did you check that the headcount reduced that way does not exceed the total of 30?
y-m-49-08.s.s2.o.b: It is impossible. The students who like at least one subject number 32, which exceeds 30
y-m-49-08.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that found the headcount of each region and compared the sum with the total.
y-m-49-08.s.s2.o.c: We cannot know. It has not been confirmed that 3 students like both subjects
y-m-49-08.s.s2.r.c: The data already says '3 students like both subjects'. You may have overlooked a given condition.
y-m-49-08.s.s2.explain: English only 17, math only 12, and both 3 add up to 32, which exceeds the total of 30. So this data is not possible (20+15−3=32>30).
y-m-49-08.s.s3.prompt: Now make it yourself. Make two different sets of survey results where the total is 50 or less, exactly 4 students like neither subject, and more students like English than math.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.hint.0: First write the relation between the number of students who like at least one subject and the total number of students.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.hint.1: Decide English, math, and the overlap x first, and then fit the total u.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.var.a: Number of students who like English
y-m-49-08.s.s3.var.b: Number of students who like math
y-m-49-08.s.s3.var.x: Number of students who like both subjects
y-m-49-08.s.s3.fail.c1: The number of students must be an integer.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.ok.c2: The number of overlapping students is 0 or more and does not exceed the size of either set.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.fail.c2: The number of students who like both subjects is 0 or more and cannot be greater than the headcount of either English or math.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.fail.c3: The total must be 50 or less.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.fail.c4: The total minus the number of students who like at least one subject is not 4.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.fail.c5: The number of students who like English must be greater than the number who like math.
y-m-49-08.s.s3.explain: For example, if (total, English, math, both)=(40, 25, 18, 7), then the students who like at least one subject number 25+18−7=36, so 4 students like neither. (30, 20, 10, 4) and (45, 30, 20, 9) also fit in the same way. Between the total and English, math, and both, there is the relation u=a+b−x+4.

y-m-49-09.title: When we only know that 'if p then q' is false
y-m-49-09.topic: Converse, inverse, and contrapositive of a proposition (what is settled and what is not settled from a false proposition)
y-m-49-09.goal: Sort out whether the truth of the contrapositive, converse, and inverse is each fixed by the information alone that 'if p then q' is false, and build cases where the converse is true and where it is false using interval conditions.
y-m-49-09.material:
For two conditions p and q, all we know is that the proposition 'proposition X: if p then q' is false, and we do not yet know what kind of conditions p and q are.
The converse is 'if q then p', the inverse is 'if not p then not q', and the contrapositive is 'if not q then not p'. Assume you have already learned that a proposition and its contrapositive always have the same truth value.
y-m-49-09.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is sufficient
y-m-49-09.thinking.1: Distinguish what is settled from what is not settled
y-m-49-09.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-09.prereq.1: Definitions of the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of a proposition
y-m-49-09.prereq.2: Truth sets of conditions given as intervals and the subset relation ('if p then q' is true ⇔ P⊂Q)
y-m-49-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the statements that we can say always hold from the information alone that proposition X is false.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write the converse and the inverse side by side using 'q, p, not', and make the contrapositive of one and compare it with the other.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one specific example where the original proposition is false and check what the converse and the inverse are like in that example.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.o.a: The contrapositive of X is also false.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.r.a: This is a choice that pointed out the property that an original proposition and its contrapositive always have the same truth value.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.o.b: The converse of X is false.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.r.b: The truth of the converse is not linked to that of the original proposition. Look at whether the converse can be true even when the original proposition is false.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.o.c: The inverse of X is true.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.r.c: The inverse is also not always linked to the truth of the original proposition. Look at whether the inverse can be false when the original proposition is false.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.o.d: We cannot know the converse and the inverse, so we cannot know the contrapositive either.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.r.d: The contrapositive is a proposition you can fix by using the property that it has the same truth value as the original proposition. This may be a judgment that did not use that property.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.o.e: The converse and the inverse of X have the same truth value as each other.
y-m-49-09.s.s1.r.e: This is a choice that checked how the converse and the inverse are related to each other (whether one is the contrapositive of the other).
y-m-49-09.s.s1.explain: The contrapositive has the same truth value as the original proposition, so it is settled as false. The converse (if q then p) and the inverse (if not p then not q) are contrapositives of each other, so they have the same truth value, but whether they are true or false is not fixed by X being false alone.
y-m-49-09.s.s2.prompt: Let p: a≤x≤b and q: c≤x≤d (x is a real number, a≤b, c≤d). Make two different p, q such that X (if p then q) is false but the converse (if q then p) is true.
y-m-49-09.s.s2.hint.0: Picture the two intervals like on a number line and tell apart the case where one is inside the other from the case where they only straddle.
y-m-49-09.s.s2.hint.1: Use the fact that for 'if q then p' to be true, the interval of q must be inside the interval of p.
y-m-49-09.s.s2.ok.c2: X is false (the interval of p does not fit entirely inside the interval of q).
y-m-49-09.s.s2.fail.c2: If the interval of p is inside the interval of q, X is true.
y-m-49-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The converse is true (the interval of q is inside the interval of p).
y-m-49-09.s.s2.fail.c3: If the interval of q does not fit entirely inside the interval of p, the converse is false too.
y-m-49-09.s.s2.explain: If the interval of p contains the interval of q but they are not equal, X is false and the converse is true. For example, if p: 0≤x≤10 and q: 2≤x≤5, then x=0 is a counterexample so X is false, but every x of q satisfies p, so the converse is true.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.prompt: In the same form (p: a≤x≤b, q: c≤x≤d), make two different p, q such that X is false and the converse is false too.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.hint.0: Draw on a number line an arrangement where the intervals of p and q do not contain each other (you may also describe the positions in words).
y-m-49-09.s.s3.hint.1: Find where the x that breaks X and the x that breaks the converse are.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.fail.c2: If the interval of p is inside the interval of q, X is true.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.ok.c3: The converse is false too (the interval of q does not fit entirely inside the interval of p).
y-m-49-09.s.s3.fail.c3: If the interval of q is inside the interval of p, the converse becomes true.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.explain: If the intervals only straddle each other (e.g., [1, 5] and [3, 8]) or do not overlap (e.g., [0, 4] and [6, 9]), both X and the converse are false. This shows with two cases that even if X is false, the converse can be true or false.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.prompt: Based on the results of the previous two steps, write why we say that the information 'X is false' alone cannot tell the truth of the converse.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.hint.0: Put the intervals you made in s2 and s3 into your sentences one at a time.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.hint.1: Compare how the result for the converse differed under the same condition 'X is false'.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Does your writing include both the case from s2 and the case from s3?
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish what is fixed by the one piece of information 'the original proposition is false' (the contrapositive) from what is not fixed (the converse)?
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.model.0: If p is [0, 10] and q is [2, 5], X is false but the converse is true, and if p is [1, 5] and q is [3, 8], both X and the converse are false. From the same information, the converse can be true or false, so it is not fixed.
y-m-49-09.s.s3.because.model.1: If the interval of p contains the interval of q, the converse is true, and if they only straddle each other, the converse is false too. For example [0, 10] and [2, 5], [1, 5] and [3, 8]. So the converse cannot be known from this information alone.

y-m-49-10.title: How far should we allow the boundary value k?
y-m-49-10.topic: Necessary and sufficient conditions (the range of a constant that satisfies a condition)
y-m-49-10.material:
There are conditions about a real number x: p: x>k (k is a real constant) and q: x²>9 (x squared is greater than 9). Three students made different claims about 'the range of k that makes p a sufficient condition for q'.
Doyun: k>3
Harin: k≥3 (k is 3 or more)
Seojun: k≥−3 (k is −3 or more)
y-m-49-10.thinking.0: Judge the boundary value (the equals sign)
y-m-49-10.thinking.1: Compare and evaluate the claims of three students
y-m-49-10.thinking.2: Explain using the case where no solution exists
y-m-49-10.prereq.0: 'H3' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment, not a grade assignment in the curriculum. Assume the learner has already studied the basic terms of the high school Common Math unit 'Sets and Propositions' (set, subset, proposition, condition, sufficient and necessary conditions).
y-m-49-10.prereq.1: Solution of the quadratic inequality x²>9 (x<−3 or x>3)
y-m-49-10.prereq.2: That 'if p then q' being true means the truth set of p is included in the truth set of q
y-m-49-10.s.s1.prompt: Which is the right range of k that makes p a sufficient condition for q?
y-m-49-10.s.s1.hint.0: Write the range of x that satisfies p for k=3 and for k=2.9, and test whether q is satisfied.
y-m-49-10.s.s1.hint.1: When k is between −3 and 3, find an x that satisfies p but does not satisfy q.
y-m-49-10.s.s1.r.a: Check whether 'if x>3, then x²>9' holds at the boundary value k=3. If it holds, there is no reason to leave out k=3.
y-m-49-10.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that checked the boundary value k=3 directly and tested whether any x breaks it when k is less than 3.
y-m-49-10.s.s1.r.c: Pick one k with −3<k<3 (e.g., k=0) and check whether there is an x with x>k and x²≤9.
y-m-49-10.s.s1.r.d: Check the direction of the inequality sign. When k=0, x=1 satisfies p, but how about q?
y-m-49-10.s.s1.explain: If k=3, then x>3, and if x>3, then x²>9 holds. If k>3, the range of p gets narrower, so it holds again. If k<3, there are values of x that are greater than k and also between −3 and 3, giving x²≤9, so it breaks. Therefore k≥3.
y-m-49-10.s.s2.prompt: This time, think about whether there is a k that makes p a 'necessary condition' for q. ('If q then p' must always be true.) Which is the right judgment?
y-m-49-10.s.s2.hint.0: Pick k from −3, 0, 3, 100 one at a time and find an x that satisfies q but does not satisfy p.
y-m-49-10.s.s2.hint.1: However small you take k, think about whether a negative x smaller than that satisfies q.
y-m-49-10.s.s2.r.a: When k=−3, x=−4 satisfies q but does not satisfy p (x>−3). Did you check the negative side of the solutions of q?
y-m-49-10.s.s2.r.b: This range is the 'sufficient condition' range from the earlier step. x=−4 satisfies q but does not satisfy p. Tell the directions apart.
y-m-49-10.s.s2.explain: The solutions of q include values x<−3 going endlessly toward the small side. Whatever k you take, x that is 1 less than the smaller of k and −4 has x²>9 but is not x>k. So there is no k for which 'if q then p' is always true.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.hint.0: Find an x that satisfies q and does not satisfy p when k is −1000 and when k is 100.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence how you choose that x depending on k.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your writing talk about 'any k' and not just one k?
y-m-49-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check directly that the x you gave satisfies q and does not satisfy p?
y-m-49-10.s.s3.model.0: Whatever value k is, if you take x to be a number less than k and also less than −3 (e.g., the smaller of k and −4, minus 1), then x²>9 but x>k does not hold. So the statement 'if q then p' is always false.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.model.1: The solutions of q include endlessly small negative numbers like −4, −5, −100, so whichever k you choose, there is a negative x smaller than it. That x satisfies q but is not x>k.
y-m-49-10.goal: Judge, taking the boundary value into account, the range of k for which x>k is a sufficient condition for x²>9, and judge with reasons whether there is a k for which it is a necessary condition.
y-m-49-10.s.s2.o.c: It is enough for k to be sufficiently small
y-m-49-10.s.s2.r.c: Check whether, however small k is, a negative x smaller than it still satisfies q but does not satisfy p.
y-m-49-10.s.s2.r.d: This is a judgment that points out that the solutions of q extend without limit to the negative side, so whatever k you choose, there is an x that breaks it.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.prompt: Write the reason for the judgment you chose in s2. Make it a reason that works for whatever value k takes, not just for one particular k.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.model.2: Whatever k is, if you take x to be -|k|-4, then x²>9 but x>k does not hold. So there is no k for which "if q then p" is always true.
y-m-49-10.s.s3.modelNote.2: An answer that determines x by an expression in k
